passage: Seema set the kitchen timer for forty minutes and pressed the button before opening her game. Weekday rule, her own: forty minutes, no more. Halfway through a tricky level her younger brother Kamal hovered, waiting for his turn on the shared tablet. With five minutes left she was one move from a treasure chest. The timer rang. Seema's thumb froze. "Just--" she began, then stopped, saved her place and handed Kamal the tablet. "Papa did not tell me to," she said, half proud, half cross. "I did." Kamal blinked. "You never stop." "Now I do." Tomorrow the treasure chest would be waiting.

qa.q: How long did Seema set the timer for?
qa.a: She set the timer for forty minutes.

qa.q: What was Seema feeling when the timer rang one move from the chest?
qa.a: Torn, half proud and half cross, since her thumb froze but she stopped anyway. 😅

qa.q: What could Seema do if the timer often rings at a bad moment in a game?
qa.a: She could choose a game or level with natural stopping points, because the limit then holds without cutting the fun short.

qa.q: How might Kamal see Seema stopping on her own?
qa.a: With surprise and probably relief, since he blinked, said she never stops, and now gets his turn.

grounding: A girl sets a forty-minute timer for weekday games and stops when it rings, so the limit feels like her own rule.

passage: Every weekday at five in their Chandigarh flat, Uma set the kitchen timer to forty minutes, put it next to the tablet and started her farm game. The first week was hard. When it rang, she'd groan, "One more harvest!" But she had made the rule herself after an argument with her mother, and she wanted to show she could keep it. So she saved and closed the game. By the third week she had started planning her forty minutes: harvest first, then build, then trade. When her cousin Amandeep visited and said, "Your mother lets you play only forty?", Uma said, "No. I let me play forty." Her mother, overhearing from the kitchen, smiled into the dal.

qa.q: How long does Uma play on weekdays?
Why did Uma stop when the timer rang, even when it was hard?
qa.a: She felt determined to prove she could keep her own rule, and proud of it being hers.

qa.q: What else could Uma do on days she wants more time?
qa.a: Save the extra wish for the weekend or agree a special day with her mother, instead of stretching the weekday timer.

qa.q: How might Uma's mother feel overhearing her?
qa.a: Pleased and proud, which is why she smiles into the dal. 😊

grounding: A girl sets a forty-minute timer for weekday gaming and stops when it rings, making the limit her own rule.

passage:
"Beep-beep-beep!"
"Lakshmi, don't stop now, we're about to win!"
"Sorry, Sonali. Timer's done."
"Your mother isn't even home. Nobody's watching."
"I know. It's my timer, not hers."
"Your timer?"
"Forty minutes on school days. I set it. If I don't, I play till dinner and end up doing homework at ten, crying."
"But we're one level from the boss!"
"Then we beat him tomorrow at four-thirty." Lakshmi saved the game. "Want to make lemon water?"
"You're weird." Sonali sighed. "Fine. But tomorrow I'm bringing snacks and we start on the dot."
"Deal. And I'll set the timer."

qa.q: How did Lakshmi feel stopping even though nobody was watching?
qa.a: Calm and firm, a little sorry to stop but proud that the rule is her own.

qa.q: What else could Lakshmi do if a level truly needs a few more minutes?
qa.a: Save it for the next day's forty minutes, as she did, rather than stretching today's limit.
Sonali is annoyed at first, calling Lakshmi weird, then agrees to start on time tomorrow.

grounding: A girl stops gaming when her own forty-minute timer rings, even with no adult watching, because the limit is her rule.
